items.prompt: Black to move after 3.Bb5. Find a sound third move.

claims.statement: 3...a6, 3...Nf6, 3...f5, 3...Nd4, 3...Be7, 3...d6, 3...Bc5 and 3...Nge7 are each within 40 cp of the engine's top choice (depth 16).

hints: The knight on c6 needs support or the bishop needs a question.
A pawn move can ask the bishop what it wants; a knight move can counterattack.
Many moves work; a6 and Nf6 are the two masters play most.
items.explain: A pawn on a6 attacks the bishop on b5 and makes it decide, while a knight on f6 attacks the pawn on e4 and ignores the bishop. Together they make up 25,233 of 26,541 master games after 3.Bb5, yet the engine rates eight third moves within 40 cp of the best one: popularity is not strength.

items.prompt: This is the Berlin endgame. Tap Black's doubled pawns.

claims.statement: Black's doubled pawns stand on c6 and c7.

hints: Doubled pawns stand on the same file.
Look at the pawns on the queenside, files a to c.
c6 and c7.
items.explain: Black recaptured on c6 with the d-pawn, so two black pawns stand on the c-file. They are weaker than separate pawns, and Black pays for the bishop pair with that structure.

items.prompt: Which side has a pawn majority on the kingside (files e to h)?

claims.statement: White's kingside pawns e5, f2, g2, h2 are a majority.
Black has three pawns on the kingside.

hints: Count the pawns on files e to h for each side.
White has e5, f2, g2 and h2.
White: four pawns against three.
items.explain: White has four pawns on the kingside (e5, f2, g2, h2) and Black has three (f7, g7, h7), because White's d-pawn captured Black's e-pawn on e5 (7.dxe5). White can try to create a passed pawn there; Black's counterweight is the bishop pair.

items.prompt: The Berlin after 6.Bxc6 dxc6. Who owns the bishop pair (two bishops of opposite square colours)?

claims.statement: Only Black owns the bishop pair.

hints: Count each side's bishops.
White traded its light bishop on c6.
Black has both bishops.
items.explain: White gave the bishop for the knight on c6 and Black retook with the d-pawn, so White has only the dark-squared bishop. Black keeps the light-squared bishop on c8 and the dark-squared bishop on f8, so Black owns the bishop pair.

items.prompt: Same opening, one move earlier: White has just taken on c6 and Black has not retaken yet. Who owns the bishop pair?

claims.statement: Both sides own the bishop pair.

hints: Count each side's bishops again.
White's bishop now stands on c6, but it is still on the board.
Both sides have two bishops.
items.explain: Until Black retakes, White still has both bishops, so each side has the pair. The pair shifts to Black only after ...dxc6 removes White's bishop.

items.prompt: Same as the first position (6.Bxc6 dxc6), but Black's h-pawn stands on h6. Who owns the bishop pair?

claims.statement: Only Black owns the bishop pair.

hints: Is the h-pawn a bishop?
The bishops have not changed.
Black still has both.
items.explain: A pawn move on the h-file does not change which bishops are on the board, so Black still owns the pair.

items.prompt: White to move. Black has retaken on c6, and the pawn on e5 is attacked once and defended by no black piece. Find a sound move.

claims.statement: 5.O-O, 5.d3 and 5.Nc3 are each within 40 cp of the engine's top choice (depth 16).
The knight on f3 attacks e5.
No black piece defends e5.
5.Nxe5 scores at least 30 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: The pawn on e5 looks free, but what can Black's queen do after the knight takes it?
Develop and castle instead; the pawn on e5 will stay under pressure.
O-O (d3 and Nc3 also work).
items.explain: The pawn on e5 is attacked by the knight and defended by nothing, yet taking it loses time: the queen goes to d4, attacks the knight and the pawn on e4, and White ends up having lost the right to castle for a pawn that Black wins back. Castling, d3 and Nc3 are sound.

feedback_by_move.f3e5: Qd4 attacks the knight and e4; after Nf3 Qxe4+ Black has the pawn back and White cannot castle.

items.prompt: Black to move after 6.d4. The knight on e4 is safe only while the e-file stays closed. Find a sound move.

claims.statement: 6...b5 is within 40 cp of the engine's top choice (depth 16).
6...exd4 scores at least 50 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
6...d5 scores at least 50 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: The bishop on a4 has been waiting since move 4.
A pawn move can attack it and gain time.
Play b5.
items.explain: The pawn on b5 attacks the bishop and forces it to move, which gains the time to support the knight with ...d5 next. Taking on d4 opens the e-file against the loose knight, and an immediate ...d5 gives White a stronger centre.

feedback_by_move.e5d4: Re1: the rook attacks the knight on e4, which is pinned to the king.
feedback_by_move.d7d5: Nxe5 and White takes the central pawn with the better game.

items.prompt: White to move. Black's knight on c5 attacks the bishop on b3, and the retreat square c2 is occupied by a pawn. Find the move that prepares the retreat and keeps the bishop pair.

claims.statement: 10.c3 is within 40 cp of the engine's top choice (depth 16).
The knight on c5 attacks the bishop on b3.
Before c3 the bishop can go only to a4, c4 or d5.

hints: Where could the bishop go, and which squares are poor?
A pawn move can open c2 for the bishop and support d4.
Play c3.
items.explain: The pawn on c3 opens c2 for the bishop and supports the push d4, so the bishop can step back or be exchanged on its own terms. Without it the bishop has only a4, c4 and the capture on d5. Other quiet moves (a4, Qe2) are within 40 cp too, because ...Nxb3 axb3 is fine for White; c3 is the most flexible, not the only move.

items.prompt: White to move. Black has just offered a pawn with ...d5. Find the move.

claims.statement: 9.exd5 is within 40 cp of the engine's top choice (depth 16).
9.Ng5 scores at least 150 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
9.Bxd5 scores at least 100 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: Black's pawn on d5 attacks your pawn on e4.
The simplest answer takes what is offered.
Play exd5.
items.explain: The pawn on e4 captures the pawn on d5, which wins a pawn and opens the e-file. The attack on h7 with the knight leaves the pawn on e4 hanging and walks into ...dxe4. The bishop capture on d5 loses material to the recapture with the knight.

feedback_by_move.f3g5: dxe4 wins a pawn and the knight on g5 is attacked.
feedback_by_move.b3d5: Nxd5 and exd5 leaves White with a weaker structure; the engine rates it far worse.

items.prompt: White to move after 7...O-O. Find a sound move that avoids the 8.c3 d5 Marshall gambit.

claims.statement: 8.a4, 8.c3, 8.h3 and 8.d3 are each within 40 cp of the engine's top choice (depth 16).

hints: Which move prevents ...d5 from being a gambit, or simply does not invite it?
A move on the a-file or the h-file, or d3.
a4, h3 or d3.
items.explain: The Marshall is the line that begins 8.c3 d5 [R]. The moves a4, h3 and d3 avoid it in that form (Black can still play ...d5 later), and the engine rates them within 40 cp of c3, so White gives up nothing in strength by avoiding the gambit.

claims.statement: 8...b4 and 8...Bb7 are each within 40 cp of the engine's top choice (depth 16).
A white pawn attacks b5.

hints: The b5 pawn is attacked by a pawn and defended by a pawn.

items.explain: The pawn on a4 attacks the pawn on b5, which is defended by the pawn on a6. Black can push the pawn to b4 and gain space, or defend it with the bishop from b7. Either is within 40 cp of the best move.
